newsitem.title: UK: MOROR RACING-BARRICHELLO GOES HOME WITH POINT TO PROVE.
newsitem.headline: MOROR RACING-BARRICHELLO GOES HOME WITH POINT TO PROVE.

text.p: Recently married, slimmer and fitter, Brazilian Formula One driver Rubens Barrichello will travel home to Sao Paulo next week with a smile on his face -- and a point to prove.

The 24-year-old, once dubbed the natural successor to fellow-Paulista Ayrton Senna, lost his way in 1995 and 1996 after crashing in practice for the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix then seeing Senna killed two days later.

Observers who had predicted a glittering career, particularly after a brilliant drive in heavy rain at the 1993 European Grand Prix at Donington, began to suggest he was a waning talent without the character to survive at the top.

But, after switching teams from Jordan to Stewart at the end of last year and marrying Sylvana Giaffone last month, he is feeling rejuvenated -- and ready to prove the early predictions about his talent were not wrong.
"I have been through a lot in my career already," he said. "I was very young when I started and then I had my crash at Imola, in 1994, and the death of Ayrton...I was not really ready for it all.

"But now, I am much tougher mentally. More like a European, if you like. Less emotional. And I feel I am stronger altogether. Changing teams to Stewart has been good for me too and I feel I am starting out afresh. It is a good feeling."
On his first outing for his new team, making its Formula One debut at the Australian Grand Prix in Melbourne, Barrichello suprised many observers with a strong, if ultimately fruitless, drive.
He had qualified 11th in his Ford-powered car and was in the hunt for a point when pushing hard in seventh position -- only for an engine failure let him down with eight laps to go.

"It was disappointing for us all, but I was glad to show what the team could do. When we have reliability I think we can score points regularly," said Barrichello. "That is a realistic prospect for us."

Next weekend, in the Brazilian Grand Prix, Barrichello will be back among his own people and hoping to deliver one of his best home performances. Last year, he was in the thick of the battle for a top six finish before spinning off.

"I know I cannot win this race, not yet anyway," he said. "But I feel that it is possible in the future. My fans want to see something from me in Brazil. But I think they know that the Stewart car is not yet ready to win races. They have to be patient for me and wait and see."
Barrichello has a special relationship with the fans at Interlagos, the sprawling but spectacular track in the outer suburbs of the massive industrial city of Sao Paulo. He grew up as one of them.

"When I was a little boy," he admitted. "I used to do what everyone else did and find holes in the fences and wriggle through. I loved the place. It is where I grew up -- my house was just down the road."

Barrichello's father was a goalkeeper for Brazilian side Santos before his son's career took off in karting and junior formula racing. Now, he follows him all over the world as he goes into his fifth grand prix season.

Barrichello also admitted that after Senna's death he felt overwhelmed by a public sense of expectation. He took Senna's death badly, found it difficult to deal with emotionally, and his own driving suffered.
But he said he was racing well last season. "It was not a bad year for me at all," he said.

"I know what some people have said and thought, but it is not true. I was driving well in a very difficult car and I was doing my best. But this move to Stewart came at the right time and I feel ready for the challenge."
